summary: Describes several cryptographic algorithms for use with the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS), which is used to sign, digest, authenticate or encrypt message content. It replaces RFCs 2630 and 3211 for this purpose and was later updated by RFCs 5754 and 8702.

eli5.summary: The CMS envelope can use different locks. This document lists which locks and keys are acceptable and how to use them.

subtitle: Which digest, signature, key-management, encryption and MAC algorithms a CMS implementation must follow, and how.

tldr.problem: The Cryptographic Message Syntax can sign, digest, authenticate or encrypt content, but it needs precise rules for how each cryptographic algorithm is identified and used so that implementations interoperate.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3370 gives, for each algorithm, its identifier, the parameters that go with it, the CMS fields where it appears and which parts are mandatory. It covers SHA-1, MD5, DSA, RSA, Diffie-Hellman, key wrapping, PBKDF2, Triple-DES, RC2 and HMAC with SHA-1.
tldr.outcome: If an implementation supports an algorithm in this document it MUST follow these rules. The RFC obsoletes RFC 2630 section 12 and RFC 3211, and was later updated by RFC 5754 and RFC 8702.

today: RFC 3370 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 2630 section 12 and RFC 3211, and it has been updated by RFC 5754 and RFC 8702. Its algorithm choices reflect 2002, so check those updates before relying on it.

sections.title: Purpose of the Document
sections.content:
The Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) is used to digitally sign, digest, authenticate or encrypt arbitrary message content. RFC 3370 is the companion that describes how common cryptographic algorithms are used with it. Implementations may support other algorithms too, but if they choose to support one described here, they MUST do so as described.

CMS values are generated using ASN.1 with BER encoding. Each algorithm has an algorithm identifier, which includes an ASN.1 object identifier, and some algorithms need extra parameters defined in an ASN.1 structure. For every algorithm the RFC states its identifier, the parameter structure if there is one, and the CMS fields where it is used.

The document separates the algorithms from the protocol. It obsoletes section 12 of RFC 2630, while RFC 3369 obsoletes the rest of RFC 2630. The split lets each be updated without affecting the other.
sections.eli5: The envelope format says how to seal a message. This note says exactly how to use each type of lock, so everyone sets them the same way.

sections.title: Message Digest Algorithms
sections.content:
Two digest algorithms are covered: SHA-1 (FIPS Pub 180-1) and MD5 (RFC 1321). Digest identifiers appear in fields such as SignedData digestAlgorithms and DigestedData digestAlgorithm. Digest values are also the input to signature algorithms.

For SHA-1, the AlgorithmIdentifier parameters field is OPTIONAL, and the correct encoding is to omit it. The RFC explains that a quirk in the translation from the 1988 to the 1997 ASN.1 syntax led some implementations to encode a NULL instead. So implementations MUST accept both absent and NULL parameters, and SHOULD generate absent parameters.

For MD5 the parameters field MUST be present and MUST contain NULL, though implementations MAY also accept absent parameters.
sections.eli5: A digest is a short fingerprint of a message. The note says exactly how to write down which fingerprint method you used.

sections.title: Signature Algorithms
sections.content:
Signature algorithm identifiers live in the SignerInfo signatureAlgorithm field, and signature values in the signature field. Two algorithms are specified.

DSA (FIPS Pub 186) MUST be used with SHA-1. DSA needs three parameters, p, q and g, carried in a Dss-Parms structure when present; if they are absent, the subject key uses the same parameters as the certificate issuer. A DSA signature produces two values, r and s, which MUST be encoded together as a Dss-Sig-Value. With id-dsa-with-sha1 the parameters field MUST be absent.

RSA (PKCS #1 v1.5) is defined in RFC 2437. Implementations that include RSA signatures MUST also implement SHA-1 and SHOULD support MD5. They MUST support the rsaEncryption identifier for signature values, and MAY support sha1WithRSAEncryption and md5WithRSAEncryption. For all of these the parameters field MUST be NULL. RSA signing produces a single value that is used directly as the signature.
sections.eli5: A signature proves who wrote a message. The note says how to write down the signing method and the signature itself so the reader can check it.

sections.title: Key Management Algorithms
sections.content:
CMS supports four ways to get the content-encryption key to a recipient: key agreement, key transport, previously distributed symmetric key-encryption keys, and passwords.

Key agreement uses X9.42 Diffie-Hellman, either Ephemeral-Static or Static-Static. The version MUST be 3. For Ephemeral-Static the sender's ephemeral public key goes in the originator field and ukm may be absent or present (implementations MUST support absent and SHOULD support present). For Static-Static, ukm MUST be present so each message between the same pair gets a different key-encryption key. Because key agreement yields a key-encryption key, a key-encryption algorithm MUST be provided for each content-encryption algorithm.

Key transport uses RSA (PKCS #1 v1.5) with block type 02, encrypting the content-encryption key; the parameters field MUST be NULL. For a Triple-DES key, the parity bits of each DES key MUST be adjusted before encryption.

Symmetric key wrap uses Triple-DES or RC2 key-encryption keys as specified in RFC 3217. When RC2 is used, 128-bit RC2 keys MUST be used as key-encryption keys, with the RC2ParameterVersion set to 58. Mixed algorithms are allowed, for example a 40-bit RC2 content-encryption key wrapped with a 168-bit Triple-DES key.

Passwords are turned into key-encryption keys with PBKDF2 (RFC 2898). Its parameters include a salt, an iteration count, an optional key length and a pseudorandom function that defaults to HMAC with SHA-1. The salt MUST use the specified OCTET STRING form.
sections.eli5: The message is locked with a key, and that key must itself reach the reader safely. The note lists four safe ways: agree on one together, lock it with the reader's public lock, use a shared secret key, or use a password.

sections.title: Content Encryption and MAC
sections.content:
For content encryption the RFC covers Triple-DES and RC2, both in CBC (Cipher Block Chaining) mode. Triple-DES is three DES operations in sequence: encrypt, decrypt, encrypt. Three-Key Triple-DES uses a different key for each; Two-Key uses one key for the two encrypt steps and another for the decrypt step. The same algorithm identifier, des-ede3-cbc, serves both. Its parameters field MUST be present and hold an initialization vector (IV) of exactly 8 octets.

RC2 in CBC mode (RFC 2268) carries an RC2CBCParameter with the rc2ParameterVersion and an 8-octet IV. The effective key bits 40, 64 and 128 are encoded as the values 160, 120 and 58. The value 160 must be written as two octets (00 A0), because the single octet A0 would represent a negative number.

For message authentication the RFC specifies HMAC with SHA-1 (RFC 2104) in the AuthenticatedData macAlgorithm field. As with SHA-1, parameters are optional: implementations MUST accept absent or NULL and SHOULD generate absent.
sections.eli5: To scramble the message itself, the note says to use a chain of locks where each block depends on the one before, plus a starting number so the same message does not scramble the same way twice. A checking code tells you if anyone changed it.

sections.title: The ASN.1 Module
sections.content: Section 7 gathers the definitions into one ASN.1 module named CryptographicMessageSyntaxAlgorithms, using IMPLICIT TAGS. It imports AlgorithmIdentifier from the PKIX module in RFC 3280 and collects the object identifiers for every algorithm in the document, plus the public key, signature value and parameter types such as Dss-Parms, RSAPublicKey, RC2CBCParameter and PBKDF2-params. The module is meant to be exported for use in other ASN.1 modules.
sections.eli5: At the end is a single master list of every lock name and shape, written in a formal language so computers can read it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC lists what implementers must protect: the signer's private key, the key management private key, key-encryption keys, content-encryption keys and message-authentication keys. Their compromise leads to masquerade or disclosure of content. Keys, IVs, one-time values such as the DSA k value, and padding must be generated randomly; weak pseudo-random number generators can leave little or no security, and the RFC points to RFC 1750 for guidance.

If the key-encryption and content-encryption algorithms differ, the effective security is that of the weaker one. For example, a 168-bit Triple-DES key wrapped with a 40-bit RC2 key gives at most 40 bits of protection, so key-encryption algorithms must be as strong or stronger.

Distribution of message-authentication keys must itself provide authentication. The RFC says RSA and Ephemeral-Static Diffie-Hellman do not provide data origin authentication, while Static-Static Diffie-Hellman does when both public keys are bound to identities in X.509 certificates. If more than two parties share a MAC key, origin authentication is not provided.

RSA PKCS #1 v1.5 encryption is vulnerable to adaptive chosen ciphertext attacks, which need an oracle that answers hundreds of thousands or more ciphertexts. This is less feasible in store-and-forward S/MIME than in interactive protocols. PKCS #1 Version 2.0 recommends OAEP padding, and designers of interactive systems should consider OAEP or avoid revealing decryption success or failure; see RFC 3218. The RFC also says algorithms weaken with time, so implementations should be modular and updated regularly.
sections.eli5: Guard your keys like house keys. A chain of locks is only as strong as its weakest one, and random numbers must really be random.
